list.listitem: All children should receive two vaccinations against measles, mumps, and rubella (MMR) separated by at least 28 days on or soon after 1 year of age, with a booster dose after 4 to 5 years of age (recommended age) or during adolescence (if second dose was not received earlier). A

Pregnant women should be tested for rubella during pregnancy. If susceptible, vaccinate in the immediate postpartum period before hospital discharge; a second dose should be administered at least one month later. B
Suspect rubella in patients with low-grade fever, suboccipital and retroauricular lymphadenopathy, and maculopapular rash spreading cephalocaudally. C
Confirm the diagnosis with a IgM-specific rubella serology, or obtain a paired serology 10 to 14 days apart for IgG-specific rubella serology. C
Treatment is supportive with rest, analgesics, and antipyretics. C

background.definition: Rubella is a viral infection characterized by low-grade temperature, mild malaise, lymphadenopathy (retroauricular or suboccipital), sore throat, headaches, and generalized erythematous maculopapular rash. Fetal infection usually results in fetal death or congenital rubella syndrome (CRS): growth retardation, microcephaly, deafness, meningoencephalitis, mental retardation, cardiac and ophtalmologic defects, hepatosplenomegaly, and purpuric-like rash.

list.listitem: Peak incidence occurs in late winter and early spring.
Most US rubella outbreaks occur where unvaccinated children and young adults gather (religious communities that refuse vaccinations, colleges, and prisons).
Highest risk for congenital rubella syndrome (CRS) occurs in Amish women (1.4/1000 live birth) compared with general US population (0.006/1000 live birth).
Widespread childhood rubella immunization has led to marked decline in both rubella infections and CRS since the early 1970s.
According to the CDC, there have been fewer than 10 cases reported annually in the US since elimination was declared in 2004; most of these are coming from outside the US.

Australia officially eliminated rubella infection in 2017. This success was attributed to a strong immunization program using MMR vaccines, the measles control campaign and the young adult MMR campaign.
In 1964 a rubella pandemic in the United States caused 12 million infections, 11,000 fetal losses, and 20,000 cases of congenital rubella syndrome.
Rubella virus is a small, enveloped, RNA virus, the only member of the rubivirus genus of the Togavirus family.
Humans are the only known host.
Acquired rubella transmission occurs via virus-containing droplets, with inhalation causing nasopharyngeal cell infection. Congenital rubella transmission occurs transplacentally.

The incubation period is 14 to 21 days (mean of 18 days) after exposure. Contagiousness is maximal one week prior and ends one week after development of rash. Therefore keep infected individual away from pregnant women and others with unknown immune status during that time period.
Reinfection is possible with milder symptoms.
All children should receive two MMR vaccinations separated by at least 28 days on or soon after age 1 year and a booster during adolescence. A

Based on a Cochrane review, MMR vaccine effectiveness against rubella, using a vaccine only used in China, is 89% (RR 0.11, 95% CI 0.03-0.42; 1 cohort study; 1621 children; moderate certainty evidence). Proven vaccination adverse effects include aseptic meningitis (for vaccines containing Urabe [risk ratio (RR) 14.28 within 3rd week] or Leningrad-Zagreb strains [RR 22.5 within 3rd week]), febrile seizure for children (attributable risk 1 per 1150 to 1 per 1700 administered doses) and possibly thrombocytopenic purpura (attributable risk 1 per 40,000 administered doses). There is no association of MMR with autism, asthma, leukemia, hay fever, type 1 diabetes, gait disturbance, Crohn's disease, demyelinating diseases, or bacterial or viral infections.

Pregnant women should be tested for rubella during pregnancy. If susceptible, they should receive MMR vaccine in the immediate postpartum period before hospital discharge; a second dose should be administered at least one month later. B
Postpubertal females without documentation of rubella immunity should be immunized unless they are known to be pregnant. A
An absolute contraindiction to rubella vaccination is pregnancy due to possible congenital infection from live virus. A
Egg allergy is no longer considered a contraindication to receive MMR vaccine. Recipients of the vaccine don't need to screened for egg allergy. A
The measles mumps rubella varicella (MMRV) vaccine combination slightly increases the risk of febrile seizure. B
Suspect rubella in patients with low-grade fever, suboccipital and retroauricular lymphadenopathy, and a maculopapular rash spreading cephalocaudally. C
A single elevated IgM-rubella specific immunoglobulin is diagnostic. C
Obtain paired serum test 10 to 14 days apart; if there is a fourfold elevation, then a presumptive case can be made. C

Differential.Differential_Features: Fever, respiratory, or gastrointestinal symptoms; aseptic meningitis
Fever, headaches, sore throat, abdominal pain; exanthem on trunk spread peripherally; face flushed with some perioral pallor, and rest of skin with erythematous rash having a "sunburn" appearance
Fever, fatigue, pharyngits, lymphadenopathy, splenomegaly, atypical lymphocytosis, and positive EBV titers
Fever, malaise, otitis media (bullous), pharyngitis, cough, pneumonia, and maculopapular rash
"Fiery" red rash on cheeks (slapped cheek appearance), followed by a soft, lacy reticular rash over rest of body, and with frequent complaint of headache, myalgia, and arthritis by adults

list.listitem: Incubation period after rubella exposure is 14 to 21 days (mean 18 days).

Prodromal symptoms begin 1 to 5 days before exanthem and consist of low-grade fever, eye pain, sore throat, arthralgia, and gastrointestinal complaints. Suboccipital and retroauricular lymph nodes are common and classic.

A rash begins in the face, spreads in a cephalocaudal direction, involving the entire body over the next 24 hours, and fades away in the next 48 to 72 hours. The rash is usually erythematous and maculopapular but may be scarlatiniform, morbiliform, or macular.
Arthritis and arthralgias are common in adolescents and adult women.

Systemic manifestation of congenital rubella syndrome (CRS) include retinopathy (60%), cataracts (27%), sensorineural defects (66%), patent ductus arteriosus (33%), pulmonary stenosis (26%), psychomotor retardation (62%), mental retardation (42%), failure to thrive (60%), microcephaly (42%), hyperactivity (18%), inguinal hernia (10%), and undescended testes (20%).

Single elevated rubella-specific IgM level is diagnostic using an enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay (ELISA). It is the preferred test. Rubella-specific IgM is found by three weeks in infected patients following development of a rash and in about 80% of patients post vaccination.
In one study, measles and rubella multiplex bead assay performed equally well compared to ELIZA and could be considered for estimating population immunity.
Alternatively, test for fourfold or greater rise in rubella-specific IgG-paired sera from acute and convalescent blood. Presumptive diagnosis can be made with this test.
Viral culture of nasopharyngeal, blood, CSF, urine, or cataract is a more specific test but more expensive and laborious.
In congenital rubella syndrome (CRS) the rubella virus can be isolated up to one year in nasopharynx, buffy coat of leukocytes, CSF, urine, or cataracts.
PCR of chorionic villous sample is an option for prenatal diagnosis.
Mild thrombocytopenia is transient and requires no therapy. Severe thrombocytopenic purpura must be monitored carefully.

Isolation of rubella virus from clinical specimen is achieved using the African green monkey kidney (AGMK) cell on an enterovirus (interference technique). This is expensive and requires technically experienced virology laboratory personnel.

WHO has recommended that all countries considering rubella control or elimination establish genetic baselines of rubella and measles viruses through characterization of endemic cases or archival samples prior to the introduction of routine immunization programs.

Suspect rubella in children with low-grade temperature, complaint of mild sore throat, eye and abdominal discomfort, suboccipital and retroauricular lymphadenopathy, and a maculopapular rash spreading cephalocaudally.
Confirm the diagnosis with rubella serology: a positive rubella-specific IgM titer, or a significant >4-fold elevation in rubella-specific IgG titers drawn at least 2 weeks apart.
Treatment is supportive with rest, analgesics, and antipyretics.
Treatment is supportive with rest, analgesics, and antipyretics. C
No treatment is available. Treatment is limited to comfort measures and antipyretics.
Use anti-inflammatory drugs and pain relievers for fever, arthralgia, and myalgia.

Immunoglobulin can modify or prevent clinical manifestations of acquired rubella. Immunoglobulin is not recommended routinely for postexposure prophylaxis of susceptible pregnant women and should only be considered if termination of pregnancy is not an option. The dose of immunoglobulin is 0.55 ml/kg via intramuscular route.
Rubella infection in children is typically a mild disease. C
If susceptible pregnant women get exposed to rubella virus during their pregnancy, the baby may be born with congenital rubella syndrome (CRS). B
CRS has a poor prognosis with high morbidity. A

Infants with CRS may have ophtalmologic (cataract, retinopathy, microphtalmos, and congenital glaucoma), cardiac (patent ductus arteriosus, peripheral pulmonary stenosis), auditory (sensorineural hearing loss), neurologic (behavioral disorder, meningoencephalitis, mental retardation), and dermal erythropoiesis (i.e., "blueberry muffin" lesions) sequelae. Mild forms can be associated with few or no obvious clinical manifestation at birth. B
See section on Screening and prevention.
An acute rubella infection in pregnancy has a maternal-fetal transmission rate greater than 80% in the first trimester and declines thereafter.
Given the high likelihood of CRS, consideration should be given to offering pregnancy termination if the infection is confirmed prior to 16-week gestational age.
Congenital defects are rare after 20-weeks gestation.
No evidence supports the use of immunoglobulins in pregnant patients exposed to rubella.
